A neural operator for predicting vibration frequency response curves from limited data
abstract: In the design of engineered components, rigorous vibration testing is essential for performance validation and identification of resonant frequencies and amplitudes encountered during operation. Performing this evaluation numerically via machine learning has great potential to accelerate design iteration and make testing workflows more efficient. However, dynamical systems are conventionally difficult to solve via machine learning methods without using physics-based regularizing loss functions. To properly perform this forecasting task, a structure that has an inspectable physical obedience can be devised without the use of regularizing terms from first principles. The method employed in this work is a neural operator integrated with an implicit numerical scheme. This architecture enables operators to learn of the underlying state-space dynamics from limited data, allowing generalization to untested driving frequencies and initial conditions. This network can infer the system's global frequency response by training on a small set of input conditions. As a foundational proof of concept, this investigation verifies the machine learning algorithm with a linear, single-degree-of-freedom system, demonstrating implicit obedience of dynamics. This approach demonstrates 99.87% accuracy in predicting the Frequency Response Curve (FRC), forecasting the frequency and amplitude of linear resonance training on 7% of the bandwidth of the solution. By training machine learning models to internalize physics information rather than trajectory, better generalization accuracy can be realized, vastly improving the timeframe for vibration studies on engineered components.

title: The numerical solution of 2D elastoplastic contact problems by dual mortar method, dualization, and optimal quadratic programming solvers
Optimal seismic design of new vertically irregular frame buildings with multi-floor isolation systems considering embedded equivalent-linear modeling
abstract: A performance-based, first-order optimization framework is presented for the seismic design of new vertically irregular frame buildings equipped with multi-floor seismic-isolation systems and supplemental viscous-dampers. The framework simultaneously optimizes the structural stiffness distribution, isolation topology, bearing types and dimensions, lead-plug diameters, viscous-damper properties, and record-dependent linearization displacements. Property modification factors are also included. Binary, discrete, and continuous design variables are treated within a gradient-based formulation. The formulation combines the Mixed-Lagrangian-Formulation, adjoint sensitivity-analysis, and Discrete-Material-Optimization. Wind resistance is enforced through a minimum number of lead-rubber bearings. Isolator shear-strain limits are also imposed. Comparison with particle-swarm-optimization produces similar design concepts with nearly three orders of magnitude fewer analyses. Five additional optimization problems are solved to examine individual design variables and modeling assumptions. The results show how the column properties, isolation topology, linearization displacements, and property modification factors affect the optimal cost and the linearized and nonlinear responses. For the investigated building and ground-motion set, the complete formulation provides the lowest-cost design that satisfies the prescribed criteria under both property bounds. Nonlinear time-history-analyses confirm satisfaction of the constraints. The present study is limited to a two-dimensional models. Equivalent-linear isolator properties are used during optimization, and a prescribed ground-motion set is considered.

title: A robust reduced order modeling of mistuned bladed disks: free interface reduction and analytical assembly
abstract: Bladed disks in turbomachinery are ideally designed as cyclically symmetric structures; however, in practice they are inevitably affected by mistuning arising from manufacturing tolerances, material variability, and service-induced damage. Even small deviations can trigger strong vibration localization and significant amplification of blade responses, making accurate mistuning analysis essential for reliable prediction of dynamic behavior and fatigue life. Although high-fidelity finite element models can capture these effects, their computational cost is often prohibitive, thus motivating the development of reduced-order models (ROMs). Most existing ROMs for mistuned bladed disks are based on fixed-interface formulations, whose retained modal properties depend on boundary conditions and are difficult to identify experimentally. To overcome this limitation, the present work introduces a free-interface-based formulation with explicit analytical assembly. In this work, a novel ROM for mistuned bladed disks is proposed, based on Rubin free-interface reduction method. The proposed framework applies free-interface reduction to the blades, i.e., the only components where mistuning is assumed to be localized. This results in ROMs with a clear physical interpretation, as the reduction basis is formed by free-interface mode shapes that can be identified experimentally without the uncertainties associated with fixture-dependent boundary conditions. An additional contribution is the explicit analytical formulation of both the reduced and assembled matrices, where all matrix partitions are fully expanded and provided in closed form. This yields a comprehensive view of the reduced system and facilitates its evaluation, particularly when computational resources are limited.

title: Discovering symbolic solutions for mechanical problems using symbolic regression and parametric regression
abstract: Symbolic regression is a machine learning-based regression technique grounded in genetic programming. It combines methodologies from multiple scientific domains to discover compact symbolic equations directly from data, without requiring predefined model structures. This makes it possible to identify complex yet interpretable relationships that may be difficult to formulate a priori. In this study, we present a novel hybrid approach that integrates symbolic regression for discovering the symbolic structure of mechanical models with conventional regression analysis for estimating the associated coefficients. Candidate structures are selected by analysing the Pareto front of symbolic expressions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across four benchmark mechanical problems.

title: A penalisation-based resolution strategy for non-associated limit analysis of discrete masonry: Performance assessment and solver benchmarking
abstract: Accounting for the non-associated flow rule in the limit analysis of discrete rigid-block masonry is challenging and often associated with numerical difficulties. In this context, this paper proposes a new resolution strategy for a 2D non-associated approach with the aim of reducing its computational complexity. The proposed strategy addresses the difficulties related to the complementarity conditions of this non-associated approach by penalising them in its objective function through a suitably selected penalty parameter. To assess its performance, this strategy is benchmarked using eight nonlinear programming (NLP) solvers against a reference strategy based on progressively relaxing the complementarity conditions through a relaxation parameter. This paper also emphasises the relevance of the proposed resolution strategy for the non-associated approach when compared with another existing iterative approach typically used to compute non-associated solutions.

An adaptive mixed-dimensional phase-field method for beam fracture
abstract: Simulating fracture in beams with high accuracy and efficiency remains a challenge within the phase-field modeling framework due to the dimensional-reduced kinematics. Traditional approach usually considers cracks to be constant over the thickness. However, when load cases involve stretching and bending, such an approach often fails to adequately capture fracture behaviors. This paper proposes an adaptive mixed-dimensional method for phase-field modeling of fracture in beams that incorporates the following features: firstly, the computational domain of beam is automatically decomposed into 'critical' and 'safe' regions according to the evolving phase-field damage variable; secondly, the local critical region where crack propagation occurs is modeled as a 2D solid, whereas the remaining safe region is represented by a simplified 1D beam model. The solid and beam models are coupled at the shared interfaces using multipoint constraint methods. By combining a 1D beam description for the majority of the structure with a 2D solid representation of the local fracture zone, the resulting model has the advantage of reducing computational cost, while still being able to accurately capture the evolution of cracks through the thickness of beams. Several numerical examples ranging from standalone beams to lattice structures test and validate the applicability of the approach.

title: A graph-based framework for casting-aware connectivity refinement in free-size optimized shell structures
abstract: Integrating casting-oriented manufacturing considerations into structural optimization remains challenging, particularly for thin-walled components optimized using free-size formulations. Such designs often exhibit spatially disconnected regions of increased wall thickness that may impair feeding accessibility and promote unfavorable solidification behavior during casting. This work proposes a graph-based framework for the connectivity refinement of free-size-optimized shell structures. Regions of increased thickness are identified and clustered, and an A*-based pathfinding algorithm is employed to establish connectivity while balancing geometric distance, required material thickening, and existing structural features. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is subsequently used to generate a globally connected and material-efficient network. The resulting connectivity paths are integrated into the structural model and preserved during a subsequent free-size re-optimization step. The framework is evaluated using benchmark examples, an industrial shock-tower demonstrator, and a complementary casting-validation study. For the industrial demonstrator, the introduced connectivity can be incorporated while maintaining the original compliance target, resulting in a final weight increase of approximately 2–4% after re-optimization. The casting-validation study further indicates that the generated connectivity can improve casting-related behavior while requiring only a limited increase in component volume. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient strategy for introducing casting-oriented connectivity into shell-based structural optimization workflows and establishes a flexible foundation for future integration of higher-fidelity manufacturing constraints and process simulations.

title: A Multi-Frequency Deep Energy Submodeling Framework for Localized High-Gradient Responses in Solid Mechanics

Predicting bifurcations in Moore–Penrose continuation using a CNN–LSTM model
abstract: Numerical continuation methods are widely used to follow solution branches of nonlinear systems, but their performance can deteriorate near bifurcation points, where correction iterations may become difficult to achieve convergence and branch-selection issues may arise. In this work, we develop a deep-learning framework for the early detection and classification of approaching bifurcations during Moore–Penrose continuation. A CNN–LSTM model is trained on stochastic time series generated from nonlinear dynamical systems exhibiting saddle-node, Hopf, transcritical, and pitchfork bifurcations. During continuation, stochastic trajectories are generated alongside the computed equilibrium branch using Euler–Maruyama integration, and the resulting time series are supplied to the trained model to obtain bifurcation predictions during the continuation process. Two sampling strategies are investigated to construct these trajectories: continuation-point sampling and adaptive parameter-space sampling. The model achieves an accuracy of 84.4% on the test set and successfully detects bifurcations in several dynamical systems not represented in the training data. The results show that adaptive parameter-space sampling can improve prediction stability when continuation points are irregularly distributed in parameter space. The proposed framework provides an online monitoring mechanism for identifying approaching bifurcations and their predicted class during continuation, thereby providing a basis for future adaptive continuation strategies.

Topology optimization of isotropic brittle materials for external-work capacity under quasi-static phase-field fracture
abstract: This paper presents a two-dimensional density-based topology optimization framework for isotropic brittle materials under quasi-static phase-field fracture. The objective is to maximize cumulative external work along a prescribed displacement history while accounting for damage evolution. A stepwise coupled sensitivity formulation with causal active-history propagation is derived from the converged displacement and phase-field equations and retains the design dependence of the maximum-history field. The complete fracture analysis is performed first, after which the recorded active branches are propagated and their material contributions are accumulated over the loading sequence. A separate full-history adjoint sensitivity formulation records the same branches during the forward solution and returns the cross-step contributions in reverse load order for directional verification. The formulation is incorporated into a SIMP-based optimization problem with a volume-fraction constraint. Directional finite-difference checks on a cantilever beam and a half-MBB beam show that the full-history adjoint sensitivity is closer to the centered difference than the Li et al. method in the prescribed direction for each case. The numerical examples present the optimized topologies, crack evolution and structural response under the prescribed loading histories.

title: A space-time boundary mapped collocation method based on tensor decomposition with adaptive temporal discretization for dynamic analyses of fluid-saturated porous media
Outlier-aware multi-fidelity surrogate-based hyperparameter optimization for topology optimization
Prediction of fibre orientation in FRC structural elements using a coupled SPH-DEM model
abstract: This study introduces a numerical framework for predicting fibre orientation in fibre-reinforced concrete (FRC) structural elements, using a coupled Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) and Discrete Element Method (DEM) approach. The methodology simulates the concrete casting process, leveraging a fibre bundling technique to enhance computational efficiency. A numerical model, implemented in Rocky-DEM with GPU acceleration, is coupled with a custom Python post-processor to assess fibre orientation and distribution within local mesh elements through 3D and 2D ellipsoidal representations. A parametric study was conducted to optimize the SPH element size and sound speed, ensuring the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The framework is validated using a benchmark of an FRC slab, demonstrating high accuracy in predicting local fibre orientation and distribution. The results highlight the method computational efficiency, particularly due to its GPU-based parallel computing implementation, which significantly reduces simulation time compared to CPU-based solvers. Compared to existing high-fidelity simulations, this study offers a practical, engineering-focused methodology that is computationally efficient and scalable for real-world FRC applications. The proposed approach is particularly well suited for the fabrication of horizontal FRC elements, with future research recommended for extending its applicability to vertical elements that are more sensitive to fibre segregation.

title: Data-driven modeling and explanatory analysis of ice-galloping in railway catenary systems considering multidimensional structural parameters
Physics-informed Bayesian identification of spatial stiffness fields in functionally graded beams from large-deflection responses
abstract: Functionally graded beams require reliable identification of spatially varying stiffness. This study presents a computational framework for stiffness identification in slender cantilever beams undergoing displacement-controlled large deflections. Large deformation is used as an information-amplifying response, and its effect on identifiability is quantified through a Fisher information matrix analysis. An energy-based physics-informed neural network (PINN) maps stiffness control values and prescribed tip displacement to curvature fields while enforcing potential energy, nonlinear kinematics, displacement constraints, and natural boundary conditions, without finite element response labels. The surrogate is validated against finite element simulations and an analytical large-deflection solver, then embedded in log-parameterised adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to reconstruct stiffness fields from synthetically noisy deformation data with credible intervals. For 400,000 samples, the surrogate reduces online MCMC time from 2700–3700 min to 11–13 min, giving a 232–284-fold speed-up. The Bayesian reconstructions recover homogeneous, linear, quadratic, and locally perturbed profiles while mitigating noise-induced deterministic overfitting. Reliable posterior exploration is obtained for the tested cases when normalised noise exceeds about 2 × 10 − 5 . The results demonstrate numerical feasibility within the adopted Euler–Bernoulli setting; experimental validation and discrepancy-aware likelihood modelling remain necessary before practical deployment.

Exact Numerical Time Integration (ENTI) of dynamic equations of motion for discretized systems subjected to Moving Load
abstract: This study presents an Exact Numerical Time Integration (ENTI) method, formulated within the exponential integrator framework, to perform “exact” dynamic analyses of discretized Linear Time-Invariant systems, toward the correct evaluation of displacement, velocity, and acceleration response variables. The method guarantees an exact time evolution of the state variables through the governing state-transition matrix expressed by an exponential matrix. One main novelty of the method lies in replacing numerical approximations of the state-transition matrix with explicit, closed-form analytical expressions of the exponential matrix for both undamped and classically damped systems. Its capabilities are illustrated for a constant-magnitude Moving Load (ML) problem on a discretized Euler-Bernoulli beam Finite Element Method (FEM) model. The Moving Load, travelling at constant speed, is modelled with equivalent nodal forces. Then, the underlying convolution integral in the general solution is solved in closed-form, thereby entirely eliminating time-discretization errors and leaving the solution solely affected by machine-precision round-off. Finally, the method is applied to a one-dimensional FEM model of the upper continuous beam of historic Paderno d’Adda Bridge (1889), under ML. Comparisons with conventional time-integration schemes show significant discrepancies, especially in acceleration responses, while ENTI remains accurate, reliable, and computationally efficient, regardless of the adopted time-step sampling.

Isogeometric analysis of the Cahn-Hilliard phase-field model coupled with strain gradient elasticity
abstract: Phase separation in solids governs microstructure evolution and, therefore, effective material properties, and is commonly modelled using phase-field approaches based on the Cahn-Hilliard equation. At small scales, size-dependent material behaviour arises that cannot be captured by classical continuum models, motivating strain gradient theories with intrinsic length scales. Despite these developments, the coupling between phase separation and gradient elasticity has remained largely unexplored beyond theoretical formulations. In the present contribution, we fill this gap by developing a numerical framework and performing a comprehensive parameter study of a phase-field model based on the Cahn-Hilliard equation coupled with strain gradient elasticity. Two weak formulations of the coupled problem are proposed, which, due to the higher-order nature of the governing equations, require C 3 or C 2 continuity for the displacement field and C 2 or C 1 continuity for the concentration field, respectively. The problems are solved using NURBS-based isogeometric analysis, which naturally provides the required higher-order continuity. We show that strain gradient effects can significantly influence the kinetics of phase separation, particularly the steady-state phase distribution under bending-type loading. The proposed model and implementation provide a robust framework for the analysis of coupled phase separation processes in materials where intrinsic length scales are relevant.

Multilevel time-space adaptive finite volume method based on energy-norm error control for transient wave propagation
abstract: A multilevel time-space adaptive vertex-centered finite volume method is presented for transient wave propagation on unstructured meshes. The method employs a hybrid reconstruction using cell-center and edge-midpoint data to improve flux accuracy while preserving local conservation. Time integration is performed with a Runge-Kutta-Chebyshev scheme in which a single global number of stages is adjusted according to the stability requirement of the semi-discrete system, enabling efficient handling of moderately stiff systems. Adaptivity is driven by a posteriori error estimates in the energy norm and implemented through a multilevel refinement strategy that allows several mesh updates within one error-assessment cycle. Mesh conformity is maintained using newest-vertex bisection. The approach achieves substantial reductions in computational cost relative to single-level adaptive methods while maintaining high accuracy in capturing propagating wavefronts and material interfaces. Benchmark tests for radial and planar waves in complex geometries confirm that the method provides improved accuracy and efficiency compared with conventional explicit and implicit schemes of similar order.

Describing function-based modal analysis
abstract: Nonlinear modal analysis provides a framework for characterising amplitude-dependent dynamic behaviour in nonlinear mechanical systems. Among existing approaches, describing function-based formulations approximate nonlinear effects through equivalent linear representations evaluated at prescribed response levels. This paper extends existing describing function-based nonlinear modal concepts to damped complex modal analysis. Nonlinear restoring and dissipative forces are represented by a complex stiffness matrix that depends on amplitude, so that the quasi-linearised structural system retains a complex characteristic equation and is treated directly as a complex eigenvalue problem that varies with amplitude. Within a fundamental-harmonic approximation, the complex eigensolution directly provides the nonlinear natural frequency, modal loss factor, and complex mode shape. Nested fixed-point and Rayleigh quotient iterations with amplitude continuation are used to trace these modal quantities at prescribed amplitudes. The formulation is assessed on representative benchmark systems using the extended periodic motion concept (EPMC) as a reference. It is further shown that both approaches yield equivalent nonlinear modal solutions under the fundamental-harmonic and single-mode assumptions adopted in this work. Overall, the framework provides a direct link between nonlinear modal analysis and classical complex eigenvalue methods, offering a physically interpretable formulation for damped nonlinear modal analysis.
